turns.prompt_text: All right so I have my Mac Mini here and I'm in Ankeny. how can I open a port so that I can SSH from Ames
turns.response_html:
Remote Access Methods for Mac Mini

Accessing a machine in Ankeny from Ames involves crossing different networks. While opening a port via Port Forwarding is the traditional method, using a Virtual Private Network (VPN) or a Mesh Overlay is generally more secure and often easier to manage.

Method 1: The Secure Mesh (Recommended)

This approach creates a secure tunnel between your devices without requiring you to touch your router's firewall settings or expose your Mac to the public internet.

  1. Install a Mesh VPN: Services like Tailscale or ZeroTier allow you to install a small client on both the Mac Mini and your remote device.
  2. Authentication: Sign in on both devices using the same account.
  3. Direct Connection: Your Mac Mini will be assigned a stable internal IP address (e.g., 100.x.y.z).
  4. Connect: Simply run ssh username@100.x.y.z from your machine in Ames.

Method 2: Traditional Port Forwarding

If you prefer to open a port directly on your router, follow these steps. Note: This exposes the SSH port to the entire internet, so ensure you have strong passwords or SSH keys enabled.

1. Enable Remote Login on the Mac Mini

  • Go to System Settings > General > Sharing.
  • Toggle Remote Login to ON.
  • Click the (i) icon to ensure your user account has access.

2. Assign a Static IP to the Mac Mini

To prevent the port from "breaking" if the Mac's local IP changes:

  • Go to System Settings > Network > Wi-Fi/Ethernet > Details... > TCP/IP.
  • Change Configure IPv4 to Using DHCP with manual address.
  • Pick an address like 192.168.1.50 (ensure it’s outside the usual DHCP range).

3. Configure the Router in Ankeny

  • Log into your router's web interface (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1).
  • Locate the Port Forwarding or Virtual Server section.
  • Create a new rule:
    • External Port: 22 (or a custom port like 2222 for "security by obscurity").
    • Internal Port: 22.
    • Protocol: TCP.
    • Internal IP: The static IP you set for the Mac Mini.

4. Identify Your Public IP

  • While in Ankeny, search "What is my IP" to get your public address (e.g., 172.x.y.z).
  • In Ames, you would connect via: ssh -p [Port] username@[Public IP].

Security Best Practices

  • Use SSH Keys: Disable password authentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and use public/private key pairs instead.
  • Change Default Port: If using Port Forwarding, use a non-standard external port (e.g., 2222) to reduce "noise" from automated bots.
  • Keep Sleep Disabled: Ensure the Mac Mini is set to "Prevent automatic sleeping when the display is off" in System Settings > Energy Saver.

How complex is your current network setup in Ankeny—are you using a standard ISP router or a custom mesh system?

turns.prompt_text: I would like to set up both tail scales so I can access it from my Mac easily but I would also like to run SSH route so that I can only use it with SSH keys
turns.response_html:
To secure your Mac Mini for remote access while using Tailscale, follow these steps to enforce SSH key-only authentication.

1. Install Tailscale

Download and sign into Tailscale on both your Mac Mini (Ankeny) and your remote Mac (Ames). Once connected, your Mac Mini will have a stable Tailscale IP (e.g., 100.x.y.z) that is only accessible to your authenticated devices.

2. Generate and Copy SSH Keys

If you haven't already, generate a key pair on your remote Mac (Ames) and send it to the Mac Mini:

  1. Run ssh-keygen -t ed25519.
  2. Copy it to the Mini: ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub username@100.x.y.z.

3. Disable Password Authentication

To ensure the route is SSH key-only, modify the SSH configuration on your Mac Mini:

  1. Open the terminal on the Mac Mini and edit the config file: sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  2. Locate and change the following lines (remove the # if they are commented out):
    • PasswordAuthentication no
    • ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
    • PubkeyAuthentication yes
  3. Save and exit (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).

4. Apply Changes

Restart the SSH daemon to force the new security rules: sudo launchctl unload /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist sudo launchctl load -w /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist

Tip: Keep your current terminal session open while testing the connection from your other Mac. This prevents you from being locked out if there is a syntax error in your config file.

turns.prompt_text: Not yet. So I did not have a SSHD config file so I created one and added the text
turns.response_html:
Since macOS handles SSH through launchd, it doesn't always ship with a pre-populated /etc/ssh/sshd_config that is easy to find, or it may rely on the default system-wide settings located in /etc/ssh/sshd_config (note the starting slash).

If you created a brand new file, we need to make sure the system is actually looking at it and that it has the correct permissions, otherwise, the SSH daemon might ignore it for security reasons.

1. Verify the File Location

The system expects the configuration at exactly: ‍/etc/ssh/sshd_config‍

If you created it elsewhere (like in your home folder), the service won't see it. You can check if it exists and see its content by running: cat /etc/ssh/sshd_config

2. Set Correct Permissions

SSH is very picky about permissions. If the config file is "world-writable," the daemon will refuse to start. Set the ownership to root and the permissions to read-only for others:

sudo chown root:wheel /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo chmod 644 /etc/ssh/sshd_config

3. Essential Config Content

Since you created a fresh file, ensure it includes these lines at a minimum to keep things functional and secure:

# Basic security
PubkeyAuthentication yes
PasswordAuthentication no
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
UsePAM yes

# macOS Specific: This allows the 'Sharing' preference pane to still work
Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*

4. Test the Configuration

Before restarting the service, you can run a "test mode" to see if the system finds any syntax errors in your new file: sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -t

If it returns nothing, your config is valid. If it returns an error, it will tell you exactly which line is causing the issue.

5. Restart the Service

To force the Mac Mini to read your new file:

sudo launchctl unload /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist
sudo launchctl load -w /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist

Warning: Since you are enforcing PasswordAuthentication no, please ensure your SSH key is fully functional. Try to SSH in from your other machine before you close your current local terminal session on the Mac Mini.

Does the sshd -t command show any errors, or does it come back clean?
